cells.literature: [L] Student self-reports of AI use did not match assessors' judgements, and 16 of 118 students claimed to have used a tool no student had accessed [R45]. Practitioners judged declarations ineffective [R24], and when 28 staff in a computer science faculty judged one fully AI-generated essay with no human-written control, 53.57% judged it mostly or wholly AI-written at once, 35.72% became suspicious only later and 10.72% had little or no suspicion, so marker suspicion is a weak check [S006]. When declarations were paired with critique and validation tasks, TAs said these exposed students who did not understand their submissions, but competence was not formally measured [R91].
cells.dataset: [D] Logged AI-use behaviour did not identify which students had larger assignment-exam gaps [J6], and no usage measure was clearly associated with exam marks [D26].
cells.interpretation: [I] A declaration records what a student says they did, not what they understand, so it needs pairing with critique tasks or a viva to verify capability.
cells.conflicts: R91 reports that validation questions within declarations exposed weak understanding (TA reports, not measured).

cells.literature: [L] Declarations do not change the underlying task, and AI-generated programming submissions scored higher than self-written ones [R96]. Reflections, logs and disclosed interactions can themselves be fabricated or mimicked [R45], [S006], [R17], [S457]. Critique tasks that require students to outperform a pre-run AI answer were reported to reduce second-guessing, but only anecdotally [R23].
cells.dataset: [D] With several prompts, GPT-4 fully answered 85.6% of CS questions [D03], and on average 14.5% of new submitted code lines matched students' own chatbot replies verbatim [J1].
cells.interpretation: [I] Declarations add transparency, not resistance; GenAI exposure depends on the task they are attached to.

cells.literature: [L] A multidisciplinary scoping review of 11 studies (only one from computing) found compliance with transparency mechanisms was often not assessed (27.3%) or relied on unverified self-disclosure (18.2%) [S423]. In computing courses, teams declaring no use were assumed truthful [R14], compliance with permitted limits could not be checked [S028], and undisclosed AI use is commonly 45-65% [R28]. Students under-declare because of fear of judgement, peer norms and low trust [S449], [S460], [S481], and fabricated declarations were observed [R45].
cells.dataset: [D] Marking did not respond to AI-authored content: moving from 0% to 100% verbatim overlap changed assignment scores by only -1.0 points [J1]. Traceability was a concern for 4 of 11 capstone clients [D20].
cells.interpretation: [I] Declarations cannot on their own establish who produced the work or how AI was used, because they rest on unverifiable self-report.

cells.literature: [L] Declarations helped a computing course team judge whether an assessment measured what was intended [R14], and validation and reflection tasks were mapped to explicit outcomes [R91]. Scales such as the AIAS set permitted AI levels according to learning outcomes [R10], [S028], [S069]. However, GenAI use can mean students show prompting skill rather than the targeted sub-skills [R51].
cells.interpretation: [I] Alignment depends on whether the declared use and any AI critique are tied to graded outcomes; a bare statement measures nothing.
cells.conflicts: R51 notes a validity threat when AI use substitutes for the targeted skill.

cells.literature: [L] Declaring, validating and critiquing AI output is linked to workplace expectations in software testing [R91] and to everyday validation of AI content [R15]. Conceptual work treats declared, scrutinised AI use as mirroring professional knowledge work [R16], [R10], [R51]. These claims are mostly author arguments and were not tested.
cells.dataset: [D] 92.7% of capstone students used GenAI in their project [D12], and 7 of 11 clients wanted GenAI use supported, though 4 of 11 named traceability as a concern [D20], [J5].
cells.interpretation: [I] Transparent AI use resembles practice, but a formal declaration is an academic artefact, so authenticity rests on the critique task more than the statement.

cells.literature: [L] In a computing course, 79% said validation tasks helped critical thinking about AI output and 61% found the declaration useful [R91]; 'allow with disclosure' was students' preferred policy and bans were rejected by over 92% [R92]. A use statement plus verification log was associated with stronger disclosure, attribution and verification practices [S140], and AI-related misconduct fell after the AIAS was introduced [S415]. However, only about one in ten students showed critical evaluation of AI [R45], and some students completed tasks only to meet the requirement [R91].
cells.dataset: [D] Verification requests were only 3.7% of students' chatbot prompts [D22], while students' own advice stressed retaining understanding and reviewing outputs [D19].
cells.interpretation: [I] Declarations with required critique are the clearest way to permit and develop responsible AI use, but the effect depends on making critique graded rather than performative.
cells.conflicts: Performative compliance [R91], low critical sensemaking [R45] and confounded misconduct counts [S415].

cells.literature: [L] Declared prompts and outputs gave educators visibility of how students approached tasks [R14], [R91], [R45], [S472]. But documentation was often poor [R72], only one of several groups fully documented prompts and outputs [R27], and about a third of logs were unusable [R17]. Logs and disclosed interactions can be mimicked or curated [S006], [S457].
cells.dataset: [D] Only 5.3% of capstone students used the university-hosted AI tool, with most using general chatbots [D14], so logs are not centrally captured.
cells.interpretation: [I] Declarations make part of the process visible, but the view is partial, student-curated and of uneven quality.
cells.conflicts: Visibility gains are offset by poor compliance and fabrication risk.

cells.literature: [L] Declarations ran in a software testing course with a typical enrolment of 150-250 students [R91], with group prompt submission for over 750 students alongside vivas [R80], and almost all of 21 universities in one sample required disclosure [S115]. The AIAS is described as quick to implement institutionally [R10]. Reviewing process logs and reflections is reported to be hard or impractical in large cohorts [R16], [S342].
cells.interpretation: [I] Collecting declarations scales easily; reading and grading detailed logs or reflections does not.
cells.cohort_note: Small (<50): full logs and reflections can be read and graded, as in a course of typically 25-35 students [R72]. Medium (50-200): feasible with rubrics and checklists, as in an 88-student module [R15] and a course of typically 150-250 students [R91]. Large (>200): simple declarations scale [R80], [S115], but detailed log review becomes impractical [R16].

cells.literature: [L] Workload or acceptability evidence for transparency mechanisms was not reported in 7 of 11 studies (63.6%) in a multidisciplinary scoping review [S423]. Some redesigns were described as lightweight or a simple change to marking criteria [R91], [R23], but markers found dual evaluation of AI and student work demanding [S108], and marking multiple drafts raised concerns [R24].
cells.interpretation: [I] A plain declaration costs little, but grading prompts, logs and critique adds marking time that has not been measured.
cells.conflicts: Lightweight claims [R91], [R23] versus reported marking burden [S108], [R24].

cells.literature: [L] Declarations were added to an existing computing course without redesigning tasks [R14], and redesign changes were reported as lightweight [R91] or a simple marking change [R23]. They need no invigilation, venues or new platforms; the main costs reported are staff time, as one faculty used champions and expert support to add standard permitted-use text to all syllabi within 4 months [S069], and staff AI literacy, which is a prerequisite [S331], [R27]. Disclosure is already near-universal in sampled guidance [S115], but a multidisciplinary scoping review found no workload or acceptability evidence in 7 of 11 studies (63.6%) [S423], and fair use may require institutions to provide premium tool access [R20] or to permit only free tools [R15].
cells.dataset: [D] Only 5.3% of capstone students used the university-hosted AI tool, with most using general chatbots [D14].
cells.interpretation: [I] A plain declaration needs little infrastructure and has low direct cost, though consistent policy, staff training and any marking of logs add staff time; cost evidence is limited, because no study measured these costs or licence spending directly.
cells.conflicts: Inconsistent policies and limited staff know-how [S006], [S482], [R27]. Markers found dual evaluation of AI and student work demanding [S108].

cells.literature: [L] Disclosure-based approaches avoid reliance on detectors, which are reported to be biased against non-native English writers [R15], [R28], [S467], and purpose-based rules can protect legitimate language support for EAL students [S457], [S028]. However, unequal access to paid tools is a recurring concern [R20], [R14], [R10], multilingual writers report stigma [S482], fear of judgement drives under-declaration [S449], and weaker writers may be disadvantaged in written reflections [R45].
cells.interpretation: [I] Declarations are fairer than detection, but their fairness depends on equal tool access and on disclosure carrying no penalty.
cells.conflicts: Language support versus stigma for multilingual students [S457], [S482].

evaluation_finding: AI-use declarations are a low-infrastructure way to permit and shape responsible GenAI use in computing assessment, although direct cost evidence is limited [R91], [R92], [S140], [R10], [S423]. They give little assurance of authorship or individual capability, because self-disclosure is often unverified, under-reported or fabricated [S423], [R45], [R28], [J1]. They work best as one layer combined with graded critique of AI output and an individual check such as a viva [R80], [R79], [R93].
strengths: Permit and develop responsible use: students valued validation tasks and preferred 'allow with disclosure' policies [R91], [R92].
Associated with stronger disclosure, attribution and verification practices when combined with logs and checkpoints [S140].
Low infrastructure and easy to add to existing tasks [R14], [R91], [S069].
Avoid reliance on biased, unreliable AI detectors [R28], [R15], [S454].
Give educators partial insight into how students used AI and help refine assessments [R14], [R45].
limitations: Rest on unverified self-report; compliance is often not checked [S423], [R14], [S028].
Students under-declare because of fear, peer norms and low trust [S449], [S460], [S481].
Declarations, reflections and logs can be fabricated or curated [R45], [S006], [S457].
Risk of performative compliance and shallow critique [R91], [R45].
Do not reduce GenAI's ability to complete the underlying task [R96], [D03].
practical_considerations: Pair declarations with graded critique of AI output and an individual viva or code walkthrough [R80], [R79], [R93].
Make disclosure safe and non-punitive, with clear task-level rules, to encourage honesty [S416], [S428], [S460].
Keep declarations short and structured for large cohorts; reserve detailed log review for small cohorts or sampling [R16], [S342], [R10].
Model the expected documentation format and weight it in the rubric, as compliance was poor otherwise [R72], [R27], [R91].
Budget for equitable tool access and staff AI literacy training, which are the main costs beyond marking time [R20], [R10], [S331], [S069].
evidence_gaps: No controlled computing study shows that declarations improve learning or integrity outcomes; S140 is non-computing and abstract-only.
Staff workload for reading and grading declarations, logs and reflections has not been measured.
No study in the pack verifies declarations against actual AI use in computing at scale.
Effects on students with disabilities or anxiety are not reported.
Most computing evidence comes from single-course practice reports of quality 2-3.
